title: Chapter 203 – Door Eight
html:
[The Lower Dock and the Black Water – Lin Jian]

The door has been waiting behind the Dock's last wall for six hundred years, and it opens for a mute girl in a patched quilted gown.

Jian stands at the bottom of the hidden stair with his staff in his right hand and a lantern in his left, and the light shakes. He has stopped trying to hide it. Both hands tremble now, a fine fast quiver that Bell calls moderate and Cheng Hui calls a family trait, and the lantern throws a nervous halo on the black stone. Beside him Mo Yan crouches at the foot of a blank wall with her palm flat against it. Her braid hangs over one shoulder. Her eyes are closed.

"You are certain?" he says.

She nods without opening them.

"It is a long way to the bottom of a mountain on a rumor."

She opens one eye and gives him a look. It says, as plainly as a spoken sentence, you are the one who asked.

Behind them Hua holds the second lantern, with her bandaged hand wrapped round the ring on its bail. She has been quiet since the Roll Room. She is thinner than she was a fortnight ago, and there is a new line between her brows, and she moves through the Hall like a woman carrying a full bowl across a crowded room. But she is steady. She is, he has begun to think, the steadiest person in the valley, which is a strange thing to think of someone who does not know her own name.

"Mo Yan says it hums," says Hua. "Door Eight."

"I have never heard it hum."

"She says it is not a sound. It is a pressure. Like the air before a thunderstorm." A faint dry smile. "I can feel it too. A little. In the mark."

Jian looks at the wall. It is black stone, smooth, cold, seamless as the others. It has no handle, no keyhole, no carving. The only thing that distinguishes it is a faint pale ring at shoulder height, no larger than a coin, where six hundred years of the Warden's lamp have never quite managed to light.

Door Eight, he thinks, and the Interface opens in the corner of his sight.

```
ARK-7 // DOOR REGISTRY
DOOR 8 .......... [UNKNOWN] -> LOCATED (LOWER DOCK)
HOLDER OF RECORD . [THE FERRYMAN]
STATE ........... DORMANT (CALLED)
REQUIREMENT ..... HOLDER OF A DOOR SIGNATURE
NOTE: THE FERRYMAN'S SIGNATURE WAS NEVER ERASED.
HOST HOLDS ARK-6 KEY. HOST MAY KNOCK.
```

May knock. He almost smiles. The thing in his head has acquired a vocabulary of courtesy.

"Step back," he says.

Mo Yan stands. Hua lifts her lantern. Jian raises his right hand, the shaking one, and lays it against the pale ring.

* * *

The decision to come down had been made three nights earlier, in a hurry, over cold barley.

Mo Yan had put her bowl down in the middle of supper and walked out of the kitchen without a word. Hua had followed. Jian had followed Hua. They had found the girl at the bottom of the Dock stair, in the blue dark, with her palm flat to the last wall and her whole small body rigid. She had not moved for an hour. When they touched her she had turned a face so white and fierce that Hua had caught her breath.

It's calling, the girl had signed. Not the Bloom. Not the tree. Another one. It says it has been waiting since the beds.

"Who?" Hua had asked.

The boatman. Mo Yan's fingers had shaped the sign slowly, with the care of a child translating a language she had only dreamed. He wants someone to tell him it's over.

Jian had stood in the Dock's cold light and looked at the wall and felt the Interface stir. Door Eight, it had said, in its small plain letters, located. He had known then that there was no way to refuse. Not out of duty. Out of the simpler certainty that a thing that has been calling for six hundred years has earned the right to be answered.

He had brought it to the Nine the next morning, in the Council Chamber, with the firewood stool pushed to the side. They had listened. Cheng Hui had asked three careful questions. Hai Ren had asked for the names of anyone who went. Duan Ke had said he would go, and Hua had said he would not, and for ten minutes the argument had gone round the stone table like a dog chasing its tail.

"A small party," Jian had said at last. "Mo Yan, because the door knows her. Hua, because the mark is a key. Myself, because the Ferryman is a holder, and the Interface can read him. Pebble, because she insisted."

"No more?" Cheng Hui had asked.

"No more. If it is a trap, I do not want to lose the Council."

"And if it is not a trap?"

"Then we shall have found a road." He had looked round the ring of grave faces. "And we shall all go down it. When we are ready. Together."

Hai Ren had written it on her slate. Together, she had written, and underlined it twice.

The wall does not open. It remembers.

That is the only word he finds for it afterward. The stone under his palm warms, then softens, then thins, until it is no more than a veil of dark mist stretched across a frame. Through it comes a smell of cold water and wet iron, and the sound of a long slow lapping, as of a very large lake against a very old pier. He feels the Interface give a small silent shudder at the base of his skull.

"Go on," says Hua.

He steps through.

The chamber on the other side is vast and low. A roof of black rock presses down a few yards over his head, unsupported, dripping. The floor is a long stone quay running away into darkness on either hand, and beyond the quay lies water: black, still, endless, with a surface like polished glass. The lantern light stops a little way out and does not come back. There are no stars. There is only the quay, the water, and a single pale post of white stone at the edge, as tall as a man, with an iron ring set in its top.

Mo Yan slips past him and runs to the post. She touches the ring. It rings, once, like a struck cup, and the sound goes out across the water and does not return.

"Do not do that," says Hua faintly.

The girl turns, abashed, and wipes her palm on her gown.

"It's all right." Jian lifts the lantern. "I think it is meant to be rung."

"By whom?"

"By anyone who wants a boat."

They wait. The silence thickens. The water laps, slow and soft, against the stone. Somewhere out on the dark a small light kindles, very far away, a yellow point like a lamp in a window. It grows. It sways. It comes toward them over the water with a slow rocking motion, and he realizes it is hung from the prow of something.

"There," breathes Hua.

It is a boat. Long, low, black-hulled, with a single mast and a furled sail the color of ashes. There is no wake. No oars dip. It glides to the quay with the soundless ease of a thing that has done it ten thousand times, and comes to rest against the white post with a kiss of wood on stone.

A man sits in the stern.

He is old, or seems so, hunched and thin in a gray hooded cloak, with a long pole across his knees and a face lost in shadow. He does not rise. He does not speak. He only turns his head, slowly, and the hood tilts toward Jian, and a pair of eyes catch the lamplight like two coins at the bottom of a well.

"Fare," says the Ferryman.

* * *

The voice is dry and quiet and entirely without malice. It is the voice of a clerk who has said one word every day for six centuries and has stopped expecting it to mean anything.

"I have no coin," says Jian.

"I do not take coin."

"What do you take?"

"What is owed." The pole shifts. "Name your crossing."

"Where does it go?"

"Up." The hood tilts. "Down. Across. It depends who asks."

"I am asking to see the road."

"That is not a crossing. That is a question." A dry rustle, like a laugh. "I do not answer questions. I carry passengers. If you wish to see the road, you must pay for the road."

Jian glances at Hua. She gives a small shrug. Mo Yan has crept up beside him and is watching the Ferryman with an expression of fierce, careful interest, as a child watches a snake in a cage.

What is the fare? he thinks.

```
ARK-7 // SCAN
SUBJECT: THE FERRYMAN (PATTERN, CONSTRUCT)
HOLDER OF DOOR 8 ... CONFIRMED
AGE ................ 631 YEARS (SIGNATURE)
STATE .............. TRANSIENT, UNMOORED
FARE STRUCTURE:
ONE CROSSING ....... ONE YEAR OF PASSENGER LIFESPAN, PER ROUTE-LEG
ROUTE: LOWER DOCK -> TERRACE ONE ... 1 LEG
ROUTE: TERRACE ONE -> TERRACE TWO ... 1 LEG
[MORE LEGS NOT DISPLAYED]
NOTE: FARE IS WAIVED FOR NINE-RING HOLDERS (TENTH SEAT).
NOTE: HOST IS A NINE-RING HOLDER.
```

He blinks. The panel has done something he did not expect: it has told him that he does not have to pay.

Why?

```
ARK-7 // EXPLANATION
THE FERRYMAN ABSORBED THE LIFESPAN OF PASSENGERS TO KEEP THE ROAD OPEN.
HE WAS A HOLDER. HE HAS NO SUCCESSOR.
A NINE-RING HOLDER MAY TAKE HIS SEAT. DOING SO ENDS THE FARE.
DOING SO ALSO MAKES THE HOLDER THE FERRYMAN.
```

The cold goes through him.

He reads it again, slowly, and then once more. The water laps. Mo Yan tugs at his sleeve.

The fare is waived, he thinks. If I become the Ferryman.

"What is it?" whispers Hua.

"A choice." He swallows. "It is always a choice."

* * *

He sits on the edge of the quay, with his legs over the water and the lantern at his side, and says nothing for a long time.

The Ferryman does not hurry him. The boat sits motionless against the post. Mo Yan has settled cross-legged on the stone beside him, chin in her hand, and Hua leans on the white post with her bandaged hand to her mouth. Nobody speaks. The only movement is the slow lapping of the dark.

"Tell me about the fare," says Jian at last.

"It is one year."

"Of whose life?"

"The passenger's."

"And where does it go?"

"Into the keel." The pole lifts and taps the black hull. "It is how the boat moves. The Founders built it so. A road of this length cannot be made of wood and wind. It must be fed with time."

"The Bloom."

"The Bloom eats matter. The road eats time." The hood tilts. "It is a gentler appetite. It was thought a fair price."

"And if a passenger cannot pay?"

"He does not cross."

"And if he crosses anyway?"

"Then he pays at the other end." The voice is flat. "With whatever he has."

Jian thinks of Ethan, kneeling in the snow, saying I am sorry. He thinks of seventy lamps. He thinks of the long thin line of the Seam, burning names and burning years, and of a road that eats time rather than people and calls it gentle.

"How many have crossed?"

"Thirty thousand, four hundred and six."

"In six hundred years?"

"In the first fifty." The Ferryman sounds almost apologetic. "The road was busy then. The Founders' people went up to build the Terraces. They did not all come back."

"And since?"

"None." The pole sinks into the water. "I have waited."

Mo Yan stirs beside him. She lifts a hand and makes a quick sign, two fingers walking along the other palm, then a fist, then a spread hand.

"Terraces," says Hua, softly. "She says they are still there."

"They are," says the Ferryman.

"Inhabited?"

The hood turns toward the girl. For the first time something like feeling creeps into the dry voice. "I cannot say. I carried the last passenger six centuries ago. But the road is not empty. I feel it, sometimes. Footsteps. Lamps." A pause. "Someone is keeping the Terraces lit."

"The Tenth," says Jian.

"I do not know the name."

"A man. Who went up."

"There was a man. He crossed in the first month. He did not pay at the other end." The pole stills. "I have wondered about him."

* * *

He asks for one crossing, to the first landing and back, and pays nothing.

That is the Ferryman's offer, once Jian has explained that he will not take the seat, not yet, not for a quay and a boat and a fare. The old man listens. He says nothing for a long time. Then he rises from the stern, tall and spare and stooped under his cloak, and holds out a hand of pale bone-colored stone.

"I have no right to offer you what you have not asked for," he says. "But I have carried the dead and the damned for six hundred years, and I find I would like to carry a living man once more before I rest. Come. I will take you as far as the first light. If you wish to turn back, you may."

"And the fare?"

"I will carry it." The voice is almost kind. "I have a great deal to spare."

Hua steps forward. "And us?"

"There is room for three."

They look at one another. Mo Yan is already at the gunwale. She hops in without ceremony and settles on the bench in the bow, with her knees drawn up and her braid over her shoulder, and looks back at them expectantly. Hua sighs. She climbs in after.

Jian goes last. The boat rocks under his weight, soft as a cradle. He sits in the middle, with the staff across his knees, and Pebble, who has been silent in his cloak all this time, wriggles out and settles on his shoulder with her claws hooked in the wool.

I am going to be sick, she observes.

"You have never been on water."

I do not intend to start.

The Ferryman pushes off with a long slow thrust of the pole, and the quay slides away.

* * *

Hua speaks first, when the black has closed round them.

She sits in the stern beside the old man, with her lantern held in her lap and her face turned toward the pole. The Ferryman does not look at her. But Jian sees his shoulders change, a small, almost imperceptible tightening, like a man who has heard his name in a crowd.

"I know you," says Hua.

"You do not."

"I do not remember." Her voice is steady. "But I know the way you hold the pole. I have seen it before. A long time ago, on a day when it rained."

The Ferryman is silent a long moment. The boat glides on.

"The day of the ring," he says at last. "You came late."

"I was with the medics."

"You had mud to the knee. You said you would not be named in the Roll." A dry, rustling sound that is almost a laugh. "I thought: there goes the only honest one of us."

"I was not honest. I chose eight children and told them it was for safekeeping."

"You chose eight children and told the Nine. That is more than most would have done."

Hua closes her eyes. "I do not know that it was right."

"Nor did I, about the road." The pole lifts and falls. "I built it to carry people up. I did not think about the ones who would be left at the bottom."

"We all did that."

"Yes." He turns his head, at last, and the hood tilts toward her, and in the lantern light Jian sees the faint outline of a long gray face, deeply lined, with a mouth that has forgotten how to smile. "That is the trouble with the Nine, Warden. We were good at building doors. We were never good at asking what we owed the ones who had to hold them."

For a time nobody speaks. The boat slides on through the dark. Then Hua reaches out, slowly, and lays her bandaged hand on the old man's gray sleeve, and the Ferryman, who has carried thirty thousand passengers across a black lake and been touched by none of them, bows his head.

The crossing takes an hour, or a minute, or a night.

He cannot tell. The black water slides past the hull without a sound. The lantern at the prow throws a small gold circle on the surface, and beyond the circle there is nothing: no shore, no sky, no horizon. The air is cold and still and tastes of iron. He sits with his hands on the staff and watches the dark, and the dark watches him.

At some point he realizes that he can hear the lake breathing.

It is not a sound. It is a movement under the boat, a vast slow rise and fall, like the chest of a sleeper. He lays a trembling hand over the gunwale and feels it through the wood. Pebble stiffens on his shoulder.

It is the Seam, she says. We are crossing it.

"The Seam is a line," says Jian.

It is a line from the other side. From this one it is a lake. Her claws flex. There is something under us. Something very large, and very old, and asleep. I would rather it stayed asleep.

"What is it?"

I do not know. But I think it is the same thing that is behind the Seventh Door. A smaller piece. A cousin.

He goes cold. He looks over the side, at the black glass. For a moment he thinks he sees a pale shape far down, a vast curved shadow, turning slowly beneath the keel.

"Do not look," says the Ferryman.

He looks away.

"The Seam is not a wall," the old man says, quietly. "It is a skin. The Bloom is on the other side, pressing. We cross it at its thinnest. But it is not thin." The pole dips. "I have carried this boat across it ten thousand times, and I have never once looked down."

"Why?"

"Because it would look back."

Mo Yan has gone very still. She sits in the bow with her palm pressed flat to the wood, her eyes huge. A tremor runs through her thin shoulders.

"Mo Yan," says Hua, sharply.

The girl lifts her hand and signs, fast and jerky. It knows us. It knows the Seven. It is saying hello.

"Who is?"

The one under the lake. The fingers shake. It says it remembers the beds.

Hua makes a small sound. She crosses the boat in two steps and takes the girl in her arms, and Mo Yan clings to her with her face buried in her shoulder.

The boat glides on. The lantern gutters. In the middle of the black water, Jian shuts his eyes, and counts his breaths, and does not look down.

* * *

The first light is a window.

It appears out of nowhere, a small square of yellow at the end of the dark, and grows as they approach until it fills the whole of his sight. Beyond it there is a quay, a real one, built of white stone and edged with iron lanterns. Beyond that, a stair. Beyond that, an arch of pale carved rock, and through the arch a glow, like the light of a city seen from a mountain.

The Ferryman brings the boat in with a long slow sweep and lays it against the quay as gently as a mother lays down a child.

"The First Landing," he says. "Terrace One. I will wait."

Jian rises. His knees are stiff. He steps onto the white stone with Pebble clinging to his collar, and the quay is solid and warm and real beneath his boots. Hua follows, then Mo Yan, who stays close to her mother. For a moment the four of them stand in the lantern light, looking at the arch.

It is carved. He sees that now. The whole face of the rock is covered in small neat figures: ships, towers, birds, a river with nine bridges. At the top of the arch, in letters a foot high, are words in a script he does not know, and below them, in a plainer hand, a line of the common tongue.

WELCOME HOME, KEYSTONE.

He reads it twice, and then a third time, because the second reading did nothing to make it less strange. Nobody in the valley has called him that. The word belongs to Mei, who has held a door for a hundred years, and to the Founders, who built the doors, and to no one else living. Whoever carved it knew the word. Whoever carved it expected someone to read it.

The words are old. The stone is weathered. But the lettering is fresh, as though freshly cut.

"Keystone," says Hua, quietly.

"Mei," says Jian.

"Or—"

"Or whoever the Founders thought would come."

Pebble claws her way up onto the crown of his head, where she has the best view.

I do not like it, she says.

"It looks like a garden."

That is what I do not like. Her scales rattle. The Hall was a garden, too, and there were seventy-three thousand sleepers under the lawn.

"It is a different place."

Everything is a different place. Until you stand in it. A snort. Tell the girl to stay behind you.

He glances down. Mo Yan has already moved. She walks at his left hand, her small shoulder against his hip, with her eyes fixed on the arch. She is not afraid. He sees that. She has the look of a child who has been told, for years, that something wonderful exists, and has just discovered it is true.

He steps forward. Under the arch the glow brightens, and he sees that it is not a city after all. It is a garden, a terraced hillside of small neat plots in silver and gold, climbing in rings toward a high bright sky that is not a sky. A smell of wet earth drifts down to him. He hears, very faintly, a bell.

Behind him the Ferryman has come to the edge of the boat and stands with his pole planted on the stone, looking up at the glow. For the first time, Jian sees his face clearly. It is old and gaunt and unspeakably tired, and it is wet.

"Six hundred years," says the old man, softly. "I told myself I was waiting for the Founders to come back. I think I was waiting for someone to say it was over."

"It is not over."

"No. But someone is there." The hood falls back. "Somebody lit the lamps. Somebody is keeping the garden. That is enough, I think, for one old boatman."

Mo Yan has crept to his side. She takes his stone hand in hers, small fingers around pale bone, and the Ferryman looks down at her and says nothing at all.

Jian lets them be. He turns back to the arch, and the garden, and the climbing rings of silver light.

And on the topmost ring, small and clear and impossible, a woman in a gray gown is standing among the lamps, looking down.

She lifts her hand.

She waves.
